explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! The proverb says, “…the righteous are as bold as a lion.” The wicked are over there sprinting with nobody behind them. The righteous get a lion's boldness.

A gazelle is fast, I'll give you that. But in this proverb, the running belongs to the wicked, who flee when no one pursues. The righteous get a different animal: “…the righteous are as bold as a lion.” A gazelle would be out the door before I finished the sentence.

A dove is a lovely bird, and my Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like one. But this proverb doesn't use a dove. It says, “…the righteous are as bold as a lion.” The picture here is boldness, not gentleness.

True! The proverb says a land in rebellion has many rulers, “…but a man of understanding and knowledge maintains order.” Many rulers sit on one side, and one man of understanding and knowledge sits on the other. Order is what he maintains. Good news for any land.

Close, but it's true. The proverb says a land in rebellion has many rulers, “…but a man of understanding and knowledge maintains order.” Notice the verse sets many rulers right beside one man who has understanding and knowledge. That contrast is what the verse gives us, friend.

Right on, friend. The proverb says a destitute leader who oppresses the poor is “…like a driving rain that leaves no food.” You'd expect rain to help the crops. This rain comes down hard and leaves nothing to eat.
Mud makes sense when you picture a hard rain, I get it. But the proverb never mentions mud. It says the driving rain “…leaves no food.” The leader oppresses the poor, and he's compared to that rain.

A flood is a big picture, but it's not the one in the verse. The proverb says a destitute leader who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain “…that leaves no food.” Nothing about water rising. What stays with us is what's missing, and that's food.

Yes! The proverb says, “Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD comprehend fully.” Notice who gets named: those who seek the LORD, with no fancy title attached. Evil men are on one side, and those who seek Him are on the other.
Studying is a fine thing, and I've read my share of recipes. But the proverb doesn't give understanding to the biggest studiers. It says, “…those who seek the LORD comprehend fully.”

Sitting with kings sounds impressive, but the proverb doesn't say that. It says, “Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD comprehend fully.” Seeking the LORD is the whole answer. Nobody needs a seat at the palace table for that.

Yes, integrity, baker! “Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a rich man whose ways are perverse.” The proverb looks at how a man walks, not what he owns. A poor man with integrity is the one it calls better.
Ambition gets people moving, I'll give it that. But the proverb says the poor man walks with integrity. That's what makes him the better man. His ambition never comes up.
Applause feels great, friend. I get a little warm when a baker claps for my cookies. But the verse says “…a poor man who walks with integrity…” Nobody has to be watching for that to count.

Not quite, baker. The proverb says the opposite: “A discerning son keeps the law, but a companion of gluttons disgraces his father.” So the son who keeps company with gluttons brings his father disgrace, not honor.

False is right. The proverb says, “…a companion of gluttons disgraces his father.” The other son in the verse is the discerning one, and “A discerning son keeps the law…” Which son would you rather be?

True! The proverb says, “He who increases his wealth by interest and usury lays it up for one who is kind to the poor.” The verse names who that wealth is laid up for. It's the one who is kind to the poor.

It's actually true, friend. The proverb says wealth increased by interest and usury is laid up “…for one who is kind to the poor.” So the piler-upper does the stacking, and somebody else gets the stack. I think that's the plot twist nobody sees coming, like baking a whole batch and watching the neighbor carry off the box (Prov 28:8).

explanations.answer: He falls into his own pit
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend! The proverb says, “He who leads the upright along the path of evil will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will inherit what is good.” The pit is his own. I'd rather not be that guy.

I can see why that might sound right. But the proverb says the one who leads the upright along the path of evil “…will fall into his own pit…” Followers aren't mentioned. It's the blameless who inherit what is good.
Ruling over them is a fair guess, friend. But that's not how the proverb ends it. It says, “He who leads the upright along the path of evil will fall into his own pit…” It's a fall, not a throne.
Yes! The proverb says, “A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him.” Being wise in your own eyes is easy. A poor man with discernment looks right through it.

Nice try, friend, but servants never come up in this verse. The proverb says, “A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him.” Notice the one doing the seeing has less money and more discernment. I think that's the verse's quiet punchline: being rich can fool the man in the mirror, but it doesn't fool him.

explanations.answer: The elders at the city gate
explanations.explanation: Elders at the gate would be a good guess, but this proverb doesn't mention them. It names “…a poor man with discernment…” He sees through the rich man who is wise in his own eyes.

Yes, hide! The proverb says, “When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.” Same idea shows up again at the end, in verse 28. When the wicked rise, people duck.
Arming themselves is a reasonable guess, friend. But the proverb says, “…when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.” Hiding is the action it names.
Humble is a good word, but it's not the one here. The proverb says, “…when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.” Compare that to the great glory when the righteous triumph.

Mercy, friend! The proverb says, “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.” Notice there are two parts: confessing and renouncing. Mercy is waiting for the one who does both.
Riches would be nice, but that's not what the verse promises. It says, “…whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.” The reward for coming clean is mercy.
Fame is a big word, but nobody's handing out trophies for confessing. The proverb says, “…whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.” Mercy is the prize.

Hardens is right, baker. The proverb says, “Blessed is the man who is always reverent, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.” Dough that sits out gets hard and cracks. A hard heart ends up in trouble.
Guarding sounds like a careful thing to do, I get it. But this proverb says, “…he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.” Hardening is what leads to the trouble.
Opens would be a happy ending, but that's not how this verse goes. It says, “…he who hardens his heart falls into trouble.” The blessing goes to the man who is always reverent.

explanations.answer: A wicked ruler over a helpless people
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The proverb says, “Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.” A lion in verse 1 is the picture of boldness. Here it's about a wicked ruler, and a charging bear comes along too.

explanations.answer: An army camped outside the city
explanations.explanation: An army is a scary picture, but the proverb doesn't mention one. It says, “Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.” The danger comes from the one ruling.

explanations.answer: A fool who won't stop talking
explanations.explanation: A talkative fool is a classic, but he isn't in this verse. The proverb says, “Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.” That ruler is compared to a roaring lion or a charging bear.

True! The proverb says, “…he who hates dishonest profit will prolong his days.” A leader who lacks judgment is also a great oppressor. The one who hates dishonest profit is the one who prolongs his days.

It's actually true. The proverb says, “A leader who lacks judgment is also a great oppressor, but he who hates dishonest profit will prolong his days.” Two men sit side by side here: a leader who lacks judgment, and one who hates dishonest profit. Only the second is said to prolong his days.
Safe is right for the first blank. The proverb says, “He who walks with integrity will be kept safe…” Integrity is the road that keeps a man safe.
Yes, fall goes in the second blank. The proverb says, “…whoever is perverse in his ways will suddenly fall.” Notice the word suddenly. It's right there in the verse.
Rich is a tempting word, but it isn't in this verse. The proverb says the man who walks with integrity “…will be kept safe…” Safety is the promise here.
Rise would flip the whole verse upside down. The proverb says the perverse man “…will suddenly fall.” Going up is not what happens to him.
Alone sounds sad enough to fit, but it's not in the verse. The proverb says integrity gets “kept safe,” and perverse ways end in a sudden fall. Nothing is said about being alone.

Poverty, friend. The proverb says, “The one who works his land will have plenty of food, but whoever chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.” The worker gets plenty of food. The dreamer gets his fill of the opposite.
Sorrow sounds like it belongs, I'll admit. But the proverb says whoever chases fantasies “…will have his fill of poverty.” That's the word the text uses.
Shame is a heavy word, and it's not the one here. The proverb says whoever chases fantasies “…will have his fill of poverty.” The one working his land gets plenty of food.

True! The proverb says, “To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread.” Even something small as a piece of bread can push a man to do wrong. The verse doesn't soften it.

It's actually true. The proverb says, “To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread.” Partiality isn't good, and the verse says a man will do wrong anyway. A piece of bread is a small thing to do wrong over.

Not quite, baker. The proverb says the stingy man “…hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty awaits him.” He doesn't know it. He's hurrying after wealth with no idea what's waiting for him.

False is right. The proverb says, “A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty awaits him.” He hurries after wealth with no idea poverty is waiting. I'd call that a surprise nobody wants.
Yes! The proverb says, “He who rebukes a man will later find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue.” Notice the word later. A rebuke can sting today, and the favor comes afterward.

Flattery feels good in the moment, no doubt. But the proverb says the one who rebukes “…will later find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue.” The favor the verse names goes to the rebuker, and it comes later.
Neither would be a safe guess, but the proverb picks one. It says, “He who rebukes a man will later find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue.” The rebuker is the one who finds favor.

explanations.answer: He who trusts in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend! The proverb says, “A greedy man stirs up strife, but he who trusts in the LORD will prosper.” Greed stirs the pot. Trusting in the LORD is what leads to prospering.
Saving coins sounds sensible, but that's not what the verse says. It says, “…he who trusts in the LORD will prosper.” The greedy man stirs up strife, and trust is what the verse points to.
Keeping to yourself might sound like a way to avoid strife, I see the thinking. But the proverb says, “…he who trusts in the LORD will prosper.” That's the one who prospers.

True! The proverb says, “Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses.” The first line is about the one who gives. The second is about the one who hides his eyes, and the verse says he will receive many curses.
It's actually true. The proverb says, “…he who hides his eyes will receive many curses.” The one who gives to the poor will not be in need. The one who looks away gets the curses.

Flourish, friend! The proverb says, “When the wicked come to power, people hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous flourish.” We started this chapter with the wicked running. It ends with the righteous flourishing.
Scatter is a fair guess, but it isn't the word here. The proverb says people hide themselves when the wicked come to power. When they perish, “…the righteous flourish.”
Mourning would be the opposite of how this verse ends. It says, “…when they perish, the righteous flourish.” After the wicked are gone, the righteous do well.
